title: Given a `List<Employee>`, sort by age ascending, and when two employees have the same age, sort those by name alphabetically. Use a chained `Comparator`.
shortTitle: Sort employees by age, and for the same age, sort by name

s1_definition.profdef: This is a two-key stable sort. The primary comparator orders by an `int` age using `Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::getAge)`, and `thenComparing(Employee::getName)` resolves ties by natural string order. `comparingInt` is preferred over `comparing` for primitive `int` keys because it avoids autoboxing each age into an `Integer`.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya at the National Bank of India wants the staff birthday list sorted youngest to oldest, and when two colleagues are the same age she wants them in alphabetical order so the list is predictable. First rule: age low to high. Tie-breaker: name A to Z.
s1_definition.oneliner: `comparingInt(age).thenComparing(name)` sorts by age, then breaks age-ties alphabetically.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This is a two-key stable sort. The primary comparator orders by an `int` age using `Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::getAge)`, and `thenComparing(Employee::getName)` resolves ties by natural string order. `comparingInt` is preferred over `comparing` for primitive `int` keys because it avoids autoboxing each age into an `Integer`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya at the National Bank of India wants the staff birthday list sorted youngest to oldest, and when two colleagues are the same age she wants them in alphabetical order so the list is predictable. First rule: age low to high. Tie-breaker: name A to Z.

**One line to remember:** `comparingInt(age).thenComparing(name)` sorts by age, then breaks age-ties alphabetically.

sections.s2_technical:
`Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::getAge)` creates a comparator keyed on the primitive age. For example, comparing an employee aged 28 against one aged 35 returns a negative number, so 28 sorts first. Using `comparingInt` instead of `comparing` matters for performance in hot paths because it extracts an `int` directly instead of boxing to `Integer`.

`thenComparing(Employee::getName)` appends the name rule, which Java only evaluates when the ages are equal. For example, if Rajesh and Amit are both 30, the name comparison decides Amit comes before Rajesh.

Natural string ordering here is case-sensitive, so a capital letter sorts before a lowercase one. If the names could have inconsistent casing, I would pass `String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER` as `thenComparing(Employee::getName, String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER)`. Because the sort is stable, any two employees identical in both age and name keep their input order.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a wellness programme that groups staff by age for health check-up slots, youngest first. Without an age sort the schedule is chaotic. This is exactly how the primary `comparingInt(getAge)` key works — it lines everyone up from youngest to oldest.

Problem 2 — Several colleagues share the same age, and the roster must be deterministic so the same slot order prints every time. This is exactly how `thenComparing(getName)` works — it breaks age-ties alphabetically so the output never shuffles.

The code has an `Employee`, a `WellnessRosterService` with `sortByAgeThenName`, and a runnable demo that logs the ordered roster.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh 30, Priya 28, Amit 30, Sneha 28, Vikram 35.

Step 1: The primary `comparingInt` key orders by age. The two 28-year-olds move to the front, the two 30-year-olds next, Vikram at 35 last.

Step 2: Within age 28, the name tie-breaker runs: Priya before Sneha. Within age 30: Amit before Rajesh.

Step 3: `toList()` builds a new ordered list; the input is unchanged.

```
INFO: Wellness roster (age asc, then name A-Z):
INFO:   age 28 | Priya
INFO:   age 28 | Sneha
INFO:   age 30 | Amit
INFO:   age 30 | Rajesh
INFO:   age 35 | Vikram
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [Rajesh/30, Priya/28, Amit/30, Sneha/28, Vikram/35]
    │
    ▼
  sorted( comparingInt(age).thenComparing(name) )
    │
    ├─ age asc → {28: Priya,Sneha}  {30: Amit,Rajesh}  {35: Vikram}
    │
    └─ within each age → name A→Z
    ▼
  toList() → NEW list
    ▼
  Output: Priya/28, Sneha/28, Amit/30, Rajesh/30, Vikram/35
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To sort by age and then by name I chain comparators. The primary key is the age, and I deliberately use `Comparator.comparingInt` rather than `Comparator.comparing` because age is a primitive int and `comparingInt` extracts it without boxing it into an Integer, which is a small but real performance and allocation win in a hot path. Then I add `thenComparing` on the name, which Java only evaluates when two employees share the same age.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this drove a wellness check-up roster that grouped staff youngest to oldest and, for people of the same age, listed them alphabetically so the slot order was completely deterministic and reproducible on every run.

The senior points I raise are that the sort is stable, so employees identical on both age and name keep their input order, and that natural string order is case-sensitive, so if the names came from an inconsistent import I would plug in `String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER` as the tie-breaker. As always, `sorted` produces a new stream and never mutates the original list.

---

keyPoints: reversed() for descending, thenComparing() for secondary sort
sorted() is stateful — buffers all elements before passing downstream
